title: A person carrying a heavy bag in one hand often leans their body towards the opposite side. What is the main mechanical reason?
question: A person carrying a heavy bag in one hand often leans their body towards the opposite side. What is the main mechanical reason?

options.text: To reduce the gravitational field around the bag.
To shift the person's combined centre of gravity and maintain balance.
To increase the bag's mass temporarily.
To eliminate the normal reaction from the ground.

explanation:
?

A. To reduce the gravitational field around the bag.  
B. To shift the person's combined centre of gravity and maintain balance.  
C. To increase the bag's mass temporarily.  
D. To eliminate the normal reaction from the ground.

**Correct answer: B**

**Explanation:** Leaning shifts the combined centre of gravity of the person and bag so that its vertical line can remain within the base of support.

title: A hollow ring and a uniform solid disc have equal outer radii and are made of the same material. Which statement about their centres of gravity is correct?
question: A hollow ring and a uniform solid disc have equal outer radii and are made of the same material. Which statement about their centres of gravity is correct?

options.text: The ring's centre of gravity lies on its circumference.
The disc's centre of gravity lies below its geometric centre.
Both centres of gravity coincide with their respective geometric centres.
The ring has no centre of gravity because its centre is empty.

explanation: Both objects have symmetric mass distributions about their geometric centres. A centre of gravity does not need to contain any material.

title: A body is cut into two pieces, and one piece is removed. Which statement about the centre of gravity of the remaining body is correct?
question: A body is cut into two pieces, and one piece is removed. Which statement about the centre of gravity of the remaining body is correct?

options.text: It must remain at the original centre of gravity.
It must shift towards the removed piece.
Its new position depends on the remaining mass distribution.
It must lie outside the remaining body.

explanation: The centre of gravity depends on how mass is distributed. Removing a portion changes the distribution, so the new centre of gravity must be determined from the remaining shape and mass.

title: Which feature distinguishes a couple from a single force acting on a rigid body?
question: Which feature distinguishes a couple from a single force acting on a rigid body?

options.text: A couple always has a non-zero resultant force.
A couple consists of equal and opposite parallel forces acting along different lines.
A couple can only act vertically.

explanation: A couple has zero resultant force but a non-zero turning effect because its equal and opposite forces act along distinct parallel lines.

title: A couple acts on a freely movable rigid body. Which effect does it produce ideally?
question: A couple acts on a freely movable rigid body. Which effect does it produce ideally?

options.text: Rotation without a resultant force causing translation.
A change in mass without motion.

explanation: The net force of a couple is zero, so it does not produce linear acceleration of the centre of mass. Its non-zero moment can produce angular acceleration.

title: Two couples have equal moments but are formed using different force magnitudes. What must be true of them?
question: Two couples have equal moments but are formed using different force magnitudes. What must be true of them?

options.text: Their forces must have equal magnitudes.
Their perpendicular separations must be equal.
The product of force magnitude and perpendicular separation must be equal.
Their directions of rotation must be opposite.

explanation: The moment of a couple equals one force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. Equal moments require equal products, not necessarily equal forces or separations.

title: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum is located between the effort and the load. Which statement is correct?
question: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum is located between the effort and the load. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The effort arm must always be longer than the load arm.
The lever can change the direction of the applied effort.
The mechanical advantage must always be less than one.
The load must always lie vertically below the fulcrum.

explanation: A first-class lever can reverse the direction of effort. Its mechanical advantage depends on the relative lengths of the effort and load arms, so it may be less than, equal to or greater than one.

title: A second-class lever is generally capable of multiplying force because:
question: A second-class lever is generally capable of multiplying force because:

options.text: The fulcrum lies between the load and effort.
The effort arm is shorter than the load arm.
The load lies between the fulcrum and effort, making the effort arm longer than the load arm.

explanation: In a second-class lever, the load lies between the fulcrum and effort. The effort arm is longer than the load arm, giving a mechanical advantage greater than one in the ideal case.

title: A third-class lever is useful even though its mechanical advantage is usually less than one. Why?
question: A third-class lever is useful even though its mechanical advantage is usually less than one. Why?

options.text: It can provide a greater range or speed of movement of the load.
It eliminates the need for effort.

explanation: In a third-class lever, the effort lies between the fulcrum and load. The load moves through a greater distance and often at greater speed than the effort point, although a larger effort is generally needed.

title: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circular path. What would happen if this force suddenly disappeared?
question: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circular path. What would happen if this force suddenly disappeared?

options.text: The body would continue along the circular path.
The body would move along a tangent to the circle at the point of release.
The body would move radially outward in a straight line.

explanation: By Newton's first law, the body continues with its instantaneous velocity. That velocity is tangential to the circular path, so the body moves along the tangent if the centripetal force disappears.

title: A stone is tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle. The string provides the centripetal force. Which statement is correct?
question: A stone is tied to a string and whirled in a horizontal circle. The string provides the centripetal force. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The force acts along the direction of the stone's instantaneous velocity.
The force acts radially towards the centre and changes the direction of velocity.
The force acts radially outward and increases the speed continuously.
The force is absent because the speed is constant.

explanation: The centripetal force acts towards the centre of the circle and continually changes the direction of velocity. In ideal uniform circular motion, it does not change the speed.

title: A body is in equilibrium under three coplanar, non-parallel forces. Which statement gives the most appropriate condition for equilibrium?
question: A body is in equilibrium under three coplanar, non-parallel forces. Which statement gives the most appropriate condition for equilibrium?

options.text: All three forces must have equal magnitudes.
All three forces must act in the same direction.
Their vector sum must be zero, and their lines of action must be consistent with zero resultant moment.
The body must have zero mass.

explanation: Equilibrium requires both zero resultant force and zero resultant moment. For three coplanar forces that are non-parallel and in equilibrium, their lines of action must meet at a common point (or be concurrent).

title: The Same Speed, a Smaller Circle
question: A particle of mass m moves at constant speed v in a horizontal circular path of radius r under centripetal force F. If the radius is halved while the speed remains unchanged, what happens to the required centripetal force?
diagramSvg:
<svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

    <text x="195" y="122" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Radius = 1 m</text>
    <text x="67" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Same speed</text>
  </svg>

options.text: It becomes four times as large.

explanation: Centripetal force F = (m × v²) / r. When mass m and speed v remain constant, F is inversely proportional to radius r (F ∝ 1/r). Halving the radius doubles the required centripetal force: F' / F = r / (r/2) = 2.

explanation:
F₁ and F₂ are perpendicular to the rod, so each produces a moment of magnitude


20×0.30=6 N m


But one tends to rotate the rod anticlockwise and the other clockwise.

F₃ is inclined at 45^°, so its moment magnitude is


20×0.30×sin45^°
≈4.24 N m


Thus F₁ and F₂ have equal magnitudes of moment but opposite turning directions.

**Concept tested:** Direction of moment and the perpendicular component of an inclined force.

title: The Weight of a Non-Uniform Metre Rule
question: A non-uniform metre rule balances horizontally on a knife edge at the 40 cm mark. A 30 N weight hangs at the 80 cm mark. The rule's weight acts at its centre of gravity, at an unknown position x. If the weight of the rule is 60 N, find x. Options
explanation:
The 30 N weight produces a clockwise moment:


30(80-40)=1200 N cm


For equilibrium, the rule's weight must act to the left of the pivot and produce an equal anticlockwise moment:


60(40-x)=1200



40-x=20Rightarrow x=20 cm


Therefore, the correct answer is actually **A. 20 cm**.

**Concept tested:** Locating the centre of gravity of a non-uniform body using moments.

title: The Lever with a Moving Fulcrum

diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="40" x2="300" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M78 84 L93 44 L108 84 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M148 84 L163 44 L178 84 Z" fill="none" stroke="#777" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><line x1="30" y1="40" x2="30" y2="72" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="30,79 24,67 36,67" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="17" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Load</text><line x1="270" y1="40" x2="270" y2="72" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="270,79 264,67 276,67" fill="#d97706" /><text x="252" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Effort</text><text x="73" y="106" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 1</text><text x="147" y="120" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 2</text></svg>

Distance of the rule's weight from the pivot:


50-45=5 cm


Distance of the suspended load:

Using the principle of moments:

W=(500 / 5)=100 N

title: Stable, Unstable and Neutral Equilibrium

All three forces produce equal moments.

explanation:
F₁ and F₂ are perpendicular to the rod, so each produces a moment of magnitude

20	imes0.30=6 N m

But one tends to rotate the rod anticlockwise and the other clockwise.

F₃ is inclined at 45°, so its moment magnitude is

20	imes0.30	imessin45°
approx4.24 N m

Thus F₁ and F₂ have equal magnitudes of moment but opposite turning directions.
concept_name: Direction of moment and the perpendicular component of an inclined force.

title: The Balance That Looks Impossible
question: A light rod is balanced on a fulcrum. A 40 N downward force acts 30 cm to the left of the fulcrum, and a 20 N downward force acts 60 cm to its right. What is the net moment?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="25" y1="48" x2="295" y2="48" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M148 91 L160 55 L172 91 Z" fill="#888" stroke="currentColor" /><circle cx="160" cy="52" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="60" y1="48" x2="60" y2="77" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M53 70 L60 80 L67 70" fill="none" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><text x="27" y="98" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">40 N</text><line x1="260" y1="48" x2="260" y2="77" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M253 70 L260 80 L267 70" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><text x="235" y="98" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">20 N</text><text x="36" y="35" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">30 cm</text><text x="226" y="35" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">60 cm</text><text x="146" y="112" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Fulcrum</text></svg>
explanation:
Left moment:

40	imes0.30=12 N m

Right moment:

20	imes0.60=12 N m

The moments are equal and opposite. Therefore, their algebraic sum is zero.
concept_name: Principle of moments and rotational equilibrium.

title: The Weight of a Non-Uniform Metre Rule
question: A non-uniform metre rule balances horizontally on a knife edge at the 40 cm mark. A 30 N weight hangs at the 80 cm mark. The rule's weight acts at its centre of gravity, at an unknown position x. If the weight of the rule is 60 N, find x.

  <line x1="50" y1="79" x2="50" y2="105" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <rect x="42" y="105" width="16" height="18" fill="#0284c7" rx="2"/>

  <circle cx="155" cy="72" r="3.5" fill="#dc2626"/>
  <line x1="155" y1="72" x2="155" y2="110" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>

explanation:
The 30 N weight produces a clockwise moment:

30(80-40)=1200 N cm

For equilibrium, the rule's weight must act to the left of the pivot and produce an equal anticlockwise moment:

60(40-x)=1200

Therefore, the correct answer is actually **A. 20 cm**.

title: A Force Acting Through the Pivot
question: A force of 40 N is applied to a body directly along a line that passes through its pivot point. What is the moment of this force about the pivot?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="30" y1="65" x2="290" y2="65" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="160" cy="65" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><path d="M145 101 L160 70 L175 101 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="160" y1="62" x2="160" y2="15" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="160,8 154,20 166,20" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="171" y="22" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">50 N</text><text x="143" y="117" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot O</text></svg>
explanation: Moment of force = Force × Perpendicular distance from pivot (F × d). When the line of action of the force passes directly through the pivot, the perpendicular distance d is zero. Hence, Moment = 40 N × 0 m = 0 N m.
concept_name: A large force can produce zero moment if its line of action passes through the axis of rotation.

title: Two Forces on a Door
question: A door of width 0.9 m is opened by applying a perpendicular force of 40 N at the handle at its outer edge. What force must be applied at a point 0.4 m from the hinges to produce the same turning effect?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="50" y="20" width="220" height="90" fill="#d8c4a3" stroke="#765b3a" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="110" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="5" /><circle cx="50" cy="43" r="4" fill="#2878c8" /><circle cx="50" cy="87" r="4" fill="#2878c8" /><line x1="270" y1="65" x2="208" y2="65" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="200,65 212,59 212,71" fill="#16856b" /><text x="212" y="54" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">40 N</text><text x="52" y="127" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Hinges (axis)</text><text x="112" y="80" font-size="11" fill="#333">Door</text></svg>
explanation: Turning effect (torque) = Force × Perpendicular distance from hinge. Initial torque M = 40 N × 0.9 m = 36 N m. For the new force F at 0.4 m: F × 0.4 m = 36 N m => F = 36 / 0.4 = 90 N.
concept_name: Inverse relationship between force and moment arm for a fixed turning effect.

title: The Unknown Support Force
question: A light horizontal rod is pivoted at a fulcrum. A load of 20 N is placed 30 cm to the left of the fulcrum. What weight W placed 50 cm to the right of the fulcrum will keep the rod in horizontal equilibrium?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 135" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="40" x2="300" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M90 82 L105 45 L120 82 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="50" y1="40" x2="50" y2="78" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="50,85 44,73 56,73" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="23" y="102" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">20 N</text><line x1="260" y1="40" x2="260" y2="78" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="260,85 254,73 266,73" fill="#d97706" /><text x="237" y="102" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">W</text><text x="38" y="28" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">30 cm</text><text x="230" y="28" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">50 cm</text><text x="91" y="99" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot</text></svg>
explanation: By the principle of moments: Anticlockwise moment = Clockwise moment. 20 N × 30 cm = W × 50 cm => 600 = 50 W => W = 600 / 50 = 12 N.
concept_name: Balancing clockwise and anticlockwise moments using consistent distance units.

title: The Suspended Triangular Lamina
question: A uniform triangular lamina is suspended freely by a pin through one of its vertices A. When it comes to rest in stable equilibrium, which of the following statements is true regarding its centre of gravity G?

options.text: Weight acts vertically downward through G, and its line of action passes through A so its moment about A is zero.
Weight acts vertically upward through G, and its moment about A is zero.
Weight acts vertically downward, producing maximum moment about A.
Weight acts along the median, but its moment is always non-zero.

explanation: A freely suspended body always comes to rest in stable equilibrium with its centre of gravity G lying vertically below the point of suspension A. In this position, the line of action of the weight passes directly through the pivot A, so the perpendicular distance is zero and the turning effect (moment) is zero.
concept_name: Centre of gravity, stable equilibrium and zero moment in the final resting position.

title: Circular Motion: The Changing Force Direction
question: A stone of mass 0.5 kg moves in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m s^. What is the centripetal force, and what happens to its direction as the stone moves?

options.text: 4 N, always tangent to the circle
8 N, directed towards the centre and continuously changing direction

title: The Centre of Gravity Shifts
question: A uniform metre rule of length 100 cm has its centre of gravity at the 50 cm mark. If a small metal weight is attached securely to the rule at the 80 cm mark, what happens to the position of the combined centre of gravity of the system?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 135" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="20" y="43" width="280" height="12" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" /><path d="M150 96 L160 57 L170 96 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><circle cx="110" cy="49" r="8" fill="#2878c8" /><circle cx="220" cy="49" r="8" fill="#d97706" /><text x="85" y="28" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">G₁</text><text x="206" y="28" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">G₂</text><text x="110" y="120" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Initial</text><text x="213" y="120" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">After adding mass</text></svg>

options.text: It shifts to the left of 50 cm.
It shifts to the right of 50 cm, towards the added mass.

explanation: The centre of gravity of a composite body is the point where the resultant weight acts. Adding a mass to the right side (at 80 cm) shifts the resultant balance point towards the added mass, to the right of 50 cm.
concept_name: Centre of gravity of a combined system.

title: The Lever with a Moving Fulcrum
question: A light horizontal lever has a load arm of 20 cm and an effort arm of 80 cm. If the fulcrum is relocated such that the load arm becomes 40 cm and the effort arm becomes 40 cm, by what factor does the effort needed to support the same load increase?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="40" x2="300" y2="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M78 84 L93 44 L108 84 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><path d="M148 84 L163 44 L178 84 Z" fill="none" stroke="#777" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><line x1="30" y1="40" x2="30" y2="72" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="30,79 24,67 36,67" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="17" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Load</text><line x1="270" y1="40" x2="270" y2="72" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="270,79 264,67 276,67" fill="#d97706" /><text x="252" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Effort</text><text x="73" y="106" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 1</text><text x="147" y="120" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot 2</text></svg>
explanation: Initial effort: E₁ = Load × (Load Arm / Effort Arm) = L × (20 / 80) = 0.25 L. After shifting the fulcrum: E₂ = Load × (40 / 40) = 1.0 L. Ratio: E₂ / E₁ = 1.0 / 0.25 = 4. Thus, the required effort becomes 4 times as large.
concept_name: How fulcrum position affects mechanical advantage and effort.

title: A Couple and Its Turning Effect
question: Two equal, opposite, and parallel forces of 10 N each act along lines separated by a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m. What is the magnitude of the moment of this couple?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="70" y="35" width="180" height="75" rx="2" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="70" y1="45" x2="20" y2="45" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="12,45 24,39 24,51" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="15" y="30" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><line x1="250" y1="100" x2="300" y2="100" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="308,100 296,94 296,106" fill="#d97706" /><text x="268" y="123" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><text x="122" y="77" font-size="12" fill="#333">Rigid body</text><text x="100" y="133" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Perpendicular separation = 0.5 m</text></svg>
explanation: The moment of a couple is defined as the product of the magnitude of either force and the perpendicular distance between their lines of action (couple arm). Moment of Couple = Force × Couple arm = 10 N × 0.5 m = 5 N m.

title: The Uniform Beam with Three Loads
question: A light horizontal beam is pivoted at its centre O. Two downward forces of 10 N and 20 N act at distances of 0.40 m and 0.10 m respectively to the left of O. What downward force acting at 0.30 m to the right of O will establish rotational equilibrium?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="45" x2="300" y2="45" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><path d="M155 93 L170 49 L185 93 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="55" y1="45" x2="55" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="55,82 49,70 61,70" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="35" y="99" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><line x1="125" y1="45" x2="125" y2="75" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="125,82 119,70 131,70" fill="#16856b" /><text x="106" y="99" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">20 N</text><line x1="270" y1="45" x2="270" y2="75" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="270,82 264,70 276,70" fill="#d97706" /><text x="250" y="99" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">W</text><text x="34" y="31" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30 cm</text><text x="105" y="31" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">10 cm</text><text x="247" y="31" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">40 cm</text><text x="146" y="111" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot</text></svg>
explanation: Total anticlockwise moment = (10 N × 0.40 m) + (20 N × 0.10 m) = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 N m. For equilibrium, Clockwise Moment = Anticlockwise Moment => F × 0.30 m = 6.0 N m => F = 6.0 / 0.30 = 20 N.
concept_name: Combining multiple moments on one side of a pivot.

question: Three identical spheres are placed in three different positions: (I) resting at the bottom of a spherical hollow bowl, (II) on a flat horizontal table, and (III) balanced at the apex of an inverted spherical bowl. Which option correctly identifies their states of equilibrium?

title: The Rotating Stone and Work Done
question: A stone tied to the end of a string is whirled in a circular path at constant speed. What is the total work done by the tension (centripetal force) in one complete revolution?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="145" cy="78" r="54" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><circle cx="145" cy="78" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><circle cx="199" cy="78" r="6" fill="#d97706" /><line x1="145" y1="78" x2="199" y2="78" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><line x1="199" y1="78" x2="199" y2="20" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="199,13 193,25 205,25" fill="#16856b" /><line x1="199" y1="78" x2="160" y2="39" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="154,33 166,37 158,45" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="208" y="25" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Velocity</text><text x="137" y="96" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">O</text><text x="17" y="146" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Velocity is tangential; force is radial.</text></svg>

options.text: Depends on the mass of the stone

explanation: Work done is given by W = F × s × cos(θ). The centripetal force (string tension) acts radially inwards towards the centre of the circle, whereas the instantaneous displacement is tangential at every point, making θ = 90°. Since cos(90°) = 0, the work done by centripetal force is always zero.
concept_name: Work done by centripetal force in uniform circular motion.

M=Fd

title: Non-Uniform Beam — ICSE 2024 Question Pattern
question: A non-uniform beam of weight 120 N is pivoted at one end. Its weight acts 20 cm from the pivot. An upward force F acts 80 cm from the pivot. Find F for rotational equilibrium.

explanation:
The weight produces a clockwise moment:

120	imes0.20=24 N m

The upward force must produce an equal anticlockwise moment:

F	imes0.80=24

F=frac{24}{0.80}=30 N

This numerical pattern is documented in the ICSE 2024 Force question collection.

title: Wheel with Three Forces — ICSE 2023 Diagram Pattern
question: Three equal forces act at point B on a wheel pivoted at A. Which force produces the maximum magnitude of moment about A?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="145" cy="88" r="62" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="145" cy="88" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><circle cx="207" cy="88" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><text x="132" y="105" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="212" y="93" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">B</text><line x1="207" y1="88" x2="207" y2="20" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="207,13 201,25 213,25" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="216" y="24" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F₁</text><line x1="207" y1="88" x2="265" y2="88" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="272,88 260,82 260,94" fill="#16856b" /><text x="257" y="76" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F₂</text><line x1="207" y1="88" x2="166" y2="129" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="160,135 164,123 172,131" fill="#d97706" /><text x="174" y="145" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F₃</text><text x="20" y="166" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Equal forces act at B; pivot is A.</text></svg>

options.text: F₂, because it acts along AB.

explanation:
The moment magnitude is

M=F rsin	heta

where 	heta is the angle between the radius AB and the force.

- F₁: 	heta=90°, so the moment is maximum.
- F₂: 	heta=0°, so the moment is zero.
- F₃: The force is inclined, so its moment is smaller than that of F₁.

concept_name: Wheel with Three Forces — ICSE 2023 Diagram Pattern

title: Wrench Length — ICSE 2011 Question Pattern
question: A man opens a nut using a wrench of length 0.4 m by applying a force of 150 N. If he can apply only 60 N to produce the same moment, what should the new wrench length be? Assume the force is perpendicular to the wrench in both cases.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 125" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="36" cy="62" r="15" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="50" y1="62" x2="285" y2="62" stroke="#777" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round" /><line x1="285" y1="62" x2="285" y2="15" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="285,8 279,20 291,20" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="245" y="15" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Force</text><text x="100" y="91" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Original length = 0.4 m</text><text x="25" y="113" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Nut / pivot</text></svg>
explanation:
Original moment:

M=150	imes0.4=60 N m

For the new wrench:

60	imes l=60

l=1.0 m

This is based on a documented ICSE 2011 question.

title: Metre Rule with Its Own Weight — Recurring ICSE Pattern
question: A metre rule of weight W balances on a knife edge at the 45 cm mark. A 20 N load is suspended at the 70 cm mark. Assuming the rule is uniform, what is its weight?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="15" y="40" width="290" height="12" rx="2" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" /><line x1="145" y1="52" x2="145" y2="89" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="145,96 139,84 151,84" fill="#2878c8" /><path d="M128 98 L145 56 L162 98 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="218" y1="52" x2="218" y2="84" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="218,91 212,79 224,79" fill="#d97706" /><text x="115" y="116" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot at 45 cm</text><text x="195" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Weight at 70 cm</text><text x="14" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0 cm</text><text x="267" y="30" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">100 cm</text></svg>
explanation:
Since the rule is uniform, its weight acts at the 50 cm mark.

Distance of the rule's weight from the pivot:

50-45=5 cm

Distance of the suspended load:

70-45=25 cm

Using the principle of moments:

W	imes5=20	imes25

W=frac{500}{5}=100 N

Therefore, the correct answer is **not among the options**; the correct value is 100 N. This illustrates why the metre rule's own weight must be included in the moment calculation.
concept_name: Combining the weight of a uniform rule with an additional suspended load.

title: The Inclined Ladder Against a Smooth Wall
question: A uniform ladder rests against a smooth vertical wall and a rough horizontal floor. Its weight is 200 N, acting at its midpoint. The horizontal reaction at the wall is 60 N. The ladder makes an angle of 45° with the floor. Find the vertical reaction of the floor, assuming the ladder is in equilibrium.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 200" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="25" y1="165" x2="295" y2="165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="245" y1="25" x2="245" y2="165" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="80" y1="165" x2="245" y2="25" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" stroke-linecap="round" /><circle cx="80" cy="165" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="245" y1="25" x2="282" y2="25" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="290,25 278,19 278,31" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="253" y="15" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Reaction R</text><line x1="165" y1="95" x2="165" y2="130" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="165,138 159,126 171,126" fill="#d97706" /><text x="174" y="119" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">W = 200 N</text><text x="37" y="185" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Floor</text><text x="258" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Smooth wall</text></svg>
explanation:
The wall is smooth, so its reaction is horizontal. It has no vertical component. Therefore, the floor must balance the entire weight vertically:

R_V-W=0

R_V=200 N

The horizontal reaction determines the frictional force at the floor, not the vertical reaction.
concept_name: Resolving forces in equilibrium when the wall is smooth.

title: A Force Applied at Different Angles
question: A rigid rod of length 0.8 m is pivoted at O. A force of 50 N acts at its free end at 60° to the rod. The force is then changed to 30 N at 90°. By how much does the moment change?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="110" x2="300" y2="110" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="35" cy="110" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><text x="20" y="130" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">O</text><line x1="35" y1="110" x2="275" y2="110" stroke="#888" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="275" y1="110" x2="225" y2="24" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="221,17 222,30 233,24" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="235" y="22" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">F = 50 N</text><path d="M245 110 A30 30 0 0 0 260 84" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><text x="250" y="101" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">60°</text><text x="105" y="100" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.8 m</text></svg>

options.text: It decreases by approximately 10.64 N m.

explanation:
Initially,

M₁=50(0.8)sin60°
=20sqrt3approx34.64 N m

Finally,

M₂=30(0.8)sin90°=24 N m

Therefore, the moment actually **decreases by 10.64 N m**. None of the options is correct.
concept_name: Comparing moments when both force magnitude and angle change.

title: The Balanced Signboard
question: A light signboard is balanced about a pivot. A 60 N load acts 0.5 m to the left of the pivot, while an unknown load W acts 1.5 m to the right. Find W.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="25" y1="28" x2="295" y2="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="45" y="28" width="230" height="12" fill="#999" /><line x1="80" y1="40" x2="80" y2="84" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="80,91 74,79 86,79" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="55" y="108" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">60 N</text><line x1="230" y1="40" x2="230" y2="84" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="230,91 224,79 236,79" fill="#d97706" /><text x="213" y="108" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">W</text><text x="57" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.5 m</text><text x="210" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">1.5 m</text><path d="M145 40 L160 75 L175 40 Z" fill="#777" stroke="currentColor" /><text x="141" y="91" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot</text></svg>
explanation:
For equilibrium, clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.

60(0.5)=W(1.5)

W=frac{30}{1.5}=20 N
concept_name: Finding an unknown load when the load arms differ greatly.

title: The Couple on a Steering Wheel
question: A driver applies a couple consisting of two equal and opposite forces of 15 N each on the outer rim of a steering wheel of diameter 0.4 m. If the driver now applies forces of 30 N each on an inner rim having a diameter of 0.2 m, what is the new moment of the couple?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="155" cy="75" r="55" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><circle cx="155" cy="75" r="6" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="100" y1="75" x2="210" y2="75" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="100" y1="75" x2="100" y2="25" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="100,18 94,30 106,30" fill="#2878c8" /><line x1="210" y1="75" x2="210" y2="125" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="210,132 204,120 216,120" fill="#d97706" /><text x="63" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">15 N</text><text x="215" y="134" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">15 N</text><text x="118" y="146" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Separation = 0.4 m</text></svg>
explanation: The moment of a couple is given by: Moment = Either Force × Arm of Couple (perpendicular distance between forces). Initial couple = 15 N × 0.4 m = 6 N m. When applying 30 N forces on an inner rim of diameter 0.2 m: New couple = 30 N × 0.2 m = 6 N m. Therefore, doubling the force while halving the couple arm leaves the moment of the couple unchanged at 6 N m.
concept_name: How two simultaneous changes affect the moment of a couple.

title: The Rod Suspended by Two Strings
question: A uniform horizontal rod weighing 120 N is suspended by two vertical strings attached symmetrically at its ends. A further 40 N weight is attached exactly at its centre. Find the tension in each string.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="20" x2="300" y2="20" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="65" y1="20" x2="65" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="255" y1="20" x2="255" y2="75" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="35" y1="75" x2="285" y2="75" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" /><line x1="160" y1="75" x2="160" y2="116" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="160,123 154,111 166,111" fill="#d97706" /><text x="173" y="110" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">120 N</text><text x="42" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₁</text><text x="263" y="12" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T₂</text></svg>
explanation:
Total downward force:

120+40=160 N

By symmetry, the two tensions are equal:

T₁=T₂=frac{160}{2}
=80 N
concept_name: Combining symmetry, force balance and the weight of a uniform rod.

title: The Child on a Seesaw Moves
question: A 30 kg child sits 2 m from the fulcrum on one side of a seesaw. A 20 kg child sits 3 m from the fulcrum on the opposite side. The seesaw is initially horizontal. The 30 kg child moves 0.5 m farther away. What happens to the net moment? Take g=10 m s^.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="45" x2="300" y2="45" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="6" /><path d="M145 92 L160 49 L175 92 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><circle cx="60" cy="36" r="9" fill="#2878c8" /><circle cx="245" cy="36" r="9" fill="#d97706" /><text x="35" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">30 kg</text><text x="220" y="20" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">20 kg</text><text x="28" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">2 m</text><text x="230" y="73" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">3 m</text><text x="140" y="108" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Fulcrum</text></svg>

options.text: It becomes 150 N m towards the 30 kg child.
It becomes 150 N m towards the 20 kg child.
It becomes 300 N m towards the 30 kg child.

explanation:
Initially, the moments balance:

300(2)=200(3)=600 N m

After moving, the first child is 2.5 m away:

M₁=300(2.5)=750 N m

The opposing moment remains 600 N m.

M_{net}=750-600=150 N m
concept_name: The effect of changing only one person's distance from a pivot.

title: The Crane Boom
question: A crane boom pivots at a fixed point. A 400 N load acts vertically downward at a horizontal distance of 3 m from the pivot. The boom itself is light. Calculate the moment of the load about the pivot.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="40" y1="135" x2="40" y2="25" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="4" /><circle cx="40" cy="95" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="40" y1="95" x2="245" y2="35" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" /><line x1="245" y1="35" x2="245" y2="83" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="245,90 239,78 251,78" fill="#d97706" /><text x="253" y="67" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">400 N</text><line x1="40" y1="95" x2="245" y2="95" stroke="#888" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><text x="115" y="112" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Horizontal reach = 3 m</text><text x="47" y="88" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot</text></svg>
explanation:
Because the load acts vertically, the perpendicular distance is the horizontal reach of 3 m.

M=400(3)=1,200 N m
concept_name: Identifying the correct perpendicular distance for a vertical force acting on an inclined boom.

title: The Door with Two Handles
question: Two people push a door at different heights. Each applies a 10 N force perpendicular to the door, in the same direction, and each force has a perpendicular distance of 0.5 m from the hinge axis. What is the total moment about the hinge?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="50" y="20" width="220" height="110" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="50" y1="20" x2="50" y2="130" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="5" /><circle cx="220" cy="50" r="5" fill="#d97706" /><circle cx="220" cy="100" r="5" fill="#d97706" /><line x1="220" y1="50" x2="265" y2="50" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="273,50 261,44 261,56" fill="#2878c8" /><line x1="220" y1="100" x2="265" y2="100" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="273,100 261,94 261,106" fill="#16856b" /><text x="235" y="40" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><text x="235" y="90" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">10 N</text><text x="85" y="145" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Two handles at different heights</text></svg>
explanation:
Each force produces

M=10(0.5)=5 N m

Since both moments act in the same rotational direction, they add:

M_{total}=5+5=10 N m
concept_name: Adding moments that act in the same direction.

title: The Horizontal Force on a Hanging Rod
question: A light vertical rod is suspended freely from its upper end. A horizontal force of 30 N is applied at a point 0.4 m below the suspension point. What is the moment of this force about the suspension point?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="160" y1="18" x2="160" y2="42" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="160" cy="43" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="160" y1="43" x2="160" y2="135" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="6" /><line x1="160" y1="90" x2="70" y2="90" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="62,90 74,84 74,96" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="72" y="77" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">30 N</text><text x="174" y="60" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Suspension</text><text x="173" y="133" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rod</text></svg>
explanation:
The horizontal force is perpendicular to the vertical rod. The perpendicular distance is 0.4 m.

M=30(0.4)=12 N m
concept_name: Calculating a turning effect about a suspension point.

title: The Load on a Wheelbarrow
question: A load of 200 N is carried in a wheelbarrow at a distance of 0.4 m from the wheel axle (fulcrum). If the effort is applied vertically upwards at a distance of 1.2 m from the axle, what is the minimum effort required to lift the load?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="65" cy="115" r="17" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><line x1="65" y1="115" x2="270" y2="45" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="5" /><line x1="135" y1="91" x2="135" y2="54" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="135,47 129,59 141,59" fill="#d97706" /><text x="143" y="58" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">Load = 200 N</text><line x1="260" y1="49" x2="260" y2="94" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="260,101 254,89 266,89" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="270" y="94" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">E</text><text x="78" y="139" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Wheel axle</text><text x="90" y="78" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.4 m</text><text x="211" y="125" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Effort arm = 1.2 m</text></svg>
explanation: By the principle of moments for a Class II lever: Effort × Effort Arm = Load × Load Arm. Effort × 1.2 m = 200 N × 0.4 m => Effort × 1.2 = 80 => Effort = 80 / 1.2 = 66.7 N.
concept_name: Mechanical advantage in a second-class lever.

title: The Nutcracker
question: A nutcracker has an effort arm of 12 cm and a load arm of 4 cm. If an effort of 30 N is applied at the outer handles, what crushing force (load) is exerted on the nut located between the jaws?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="55" cy="120" r="9" fill="#888" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="55" y1="120" x2="260" y2="60" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="6" stroke-linecap="round" /><line x1="55" y1="120" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="6" stroke-linecap="round" /><circle cx="180" cy="89" r="10" fill="#b77935" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="260" y1="60" x2="260" y2="25" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="260,18 254,30 266,30" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="268" y="29" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="14" y="144" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Hinge</text><text x="170" y="72" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Nut</text><text x="82" y="101" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">4 cm</text><text x="199" y="144" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">12 cm</text></svg>
explanation: For an ideal Class II lever: Load × Load Arm = Effort × Effort Arm. Load × 4 cm = 30 N × 12 cm => Load × 4 = 360 => Load = 360 / 4 = 90 N.
concept_name: Force multiplication in a compound-use lever.

title: The Bottle Opener
question: A bottle opener of length 10 cm is used to open a bottle cap requiring a lifting force of 120 N. If the cap is situated at 2.0 cm from the fulcrum, what minimum effort must be applied at the end of the handle?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="90" width="110" height="35" rx="5" fill="#aaa" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="65" y="65" width="35" height="25" fill="#777" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="82" y1="68" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round" /><circle cx="82" cy="68" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="260" y1="35" x2="260" y2="4" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="260,-2 254,10 266,10" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="269" y="14" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="29" y="139" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Bottle cap</text><text x="99" y="58" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Fulcrum</text></svg>
explanation: By the principle of moments: Effort × Effort Arm = Load × Load Arm. Effort × 10 cm = 120 N × 2 cm => Effort × 10 = 240 => Effort = 240 / 10 = 24 N.
concept_name: Finding the effort required to overcome a known load.

title: The Force at the Edge of a Disc
question: A uniform circular disc of radius 0.3 m is pivoted at its centre. A tangential force applied at its circumference is reduced from 20 N to 15 N. By what amount does the torque (moment of force) acting on the disc decrease?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="145" cy="78" r="55" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="145" cy="78" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="145" y1="78" x2="200" y2="78" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><line x1="200" y1="78" x2="200" y2="15" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="200,8 194,20 206,20" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="209" y="18" font-size="12" fill="currentColor">20 N</text><text x="160" y="69" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">0.3 m</text><text x="133" y="95" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">O</text></svg>
explanation: Initial moment: M₁ = F₁ × r = 20 N × 0.3 m = 6.0 N m. Final moment: M₂ = F₂ × r = 15 N × 0.3 m = 4.5 N m. Decrease in moment: ΔM = M₁ - M₂ = 6.0 - 4.5 = 1.5 N m.
concept_name: Change in moment when a tangential force changes.

title: A Uniform Metre Rule with an Off-Centre Pivot
question: A uniform metre rule of weight 4.0 N is pivoted at the 65 cm mark. What is the magnitude of the moment produced by the rule's own weight about this pivot?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="20" y1="45" x2="300" y2="45" stroke="#b77935" stroke-width="7" /><circle cx="200" cy="45" r="5" fill="currentColor" /><path d="M185 90 L200 50 L215 90 Z" fill="#999" stroke="currentColor" /><line x1="160" y1="45" x2="160" y2="82" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><polygon points="160,89 154,77 166,77" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="142" y="107" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Weight W</text><text x="83" y="31" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Centre at 50 cm</text><text x="185" y="109" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Pivot at 65 cm</text></svg>
explanation: The weight of a uniform 100 cm metre rule acts through its centre of gravity at the 50 cm mark. Distance from pivot (65 cm) = 65 cm - 50 cm = 15 cm = 0.15 m. Moment of weight = Force × Distance = 4.0 N × 0.15 m = 0.60 N m (acting anticlockwise).
concept_name: Moment produced by a body's own weight when the pivot is not at its centre.

title: The Spinning Fan Blade
question: A ceiling fan rotates about its central axis at a constant speed. Which of the following statements correctly describes the velocity and acceleration of a point located at the outer tip of a blade?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="155" cy="78" r="8" fill="currentColor" /><path d="M155 70 Q145 30 120 25 Q132 59 155 70" fill="#2878c8" stroke="#2878c8" /><path d="M163 78 Q202 68 207 43 Q178 50 163 78" fill="#2878c8" stroke="#2878c8" /><path d="M155 86 Q165 126 190 131 Q178 97 155 86" fill="#2878c8" stroke="#2878c8" /><path d="M147 78 Q108 88 103 113 Q132 106 147 78" fill="#2878c8" stroke="#2878c8" /><path d="M220 80 A65 65 0 0 0 169 17" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="165,17 178,17 171,28" fill="#d97706" /><text x="222" y="70" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Rotation</text></svg>

options.text: Its velocity is directed towards the centre.
Its acceleration is zero because its speed is constant.
Its velocity is tangential, and its centripetal acceleration is directed towards the centre.
Its acceleration is tangential and directed away from the centre.

explanation: In uniform circular motion, the speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes continuously, remaining tangential to the circular path at every point. This continuous change in velocity gives rise to centripetal acceleration, which is directed radially inwards towards the centre of rotation.
concept_name: Distinguishing velocity direction from centripetal acceleration.

title: The Stone Whirled on a String
question: A stone of mass 0.2 kg is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m with a constant speed of 5.0 m/s. What is the tension in the string that provides the necessary centripetal force?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="140" cy="80" r="55" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><circle cx="140" cy="80" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><circle cx="195" cy="80" r="7" fill="#d97706" /><line x1="140" y1="80" x2="195" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="195" y1="80" x2="195" y2="18" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="195,11 189,23 201,23" fill="#2878c8" /><text x="203" y="24" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">v</text><line x1="195" y1="80" x2="155" y2="80" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="148,80 160,74 160,86" fill="#16856b" /><text x="163" y="70" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">T</text><text x="130" y="98" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">O</text><text x="145" y="68" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">r</text></svg>
explanation: Centripetal force F_c = (m × v²) / r = (0.2 × 5²) / 0.5 = (0.2 × 25) / 0.5 = 5.0 / 0.5 = 10 N. The string tension supplies this required centripetal force.
concept_name: Calculating the force needed to maintain circular motion.

title: What Happens When the String Breaks?
question: A stone tied to the end of a string is whirled in a horizontal circular path. If the string suddenly snaps, along which path will the stone fly off?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="125" cy="80" r="48" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 4" /><circle cx="173" cy="80" r="6" fill="#d97706" /><circle cx="125" cy="80" r="4" fill="currentColor" /><line x1="125" y1="80" x2="173" y2="80" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><line x1="173" y1="80" x2="173" y2="24" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="173,17 167,29 179,29" fill="#16856b" /><text x="182" y="27" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Instantaneous velocity</text><path d="M173 80 Q215 62 245 40" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><text x="190" y="102" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">After release</text></svg>

options.text: Directly towards the centre of the circle.
Directly away from the centre along the radius.
Along the tangent to the circular path at the instant of breaking.
Along the circular path for a few revolutions.

explanation: The string supplies the inward centripetal force that keeps the stone in circular motion. Once the string breaks, this force ceases to act. By Newton's first law of motion (inertia of direction), the stone continues to move along a straight line tangent to the circular path at that instant.
concept_name: Inertia and the instantaneous direction of motion in circular motion.

title: The Same Speed, a Smaller Circle
question: A particle of mass m moves at constant speed v in a horizontal circular path of radius r under centripetal force F. If the radius is halved while the speed remains unchanged, what happens to the required centripetal force?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="95" cy="78" r="48" fill="none" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="230" cy="78" r="28" fill="none" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="143" cy="78" r="5" fill="#2878c8" /><circle cx="258" cy="78" r="5" fill="#d97706" /><text x="58" y="145" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Radius = 2 m</text><text x="195" y="122" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Radius = 1 m</text><text x="67" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Same speed</text></svg>

options.text: It becomes four times as large.

explanation: Centripetal force F = (m × v²) / r. When mass m and speed v remain constant, F is inversely proportional to radius r (F ∝ 1/r). Halving the radius doubles the required centripetal force: F' / F = r / (r/2) = 2.
concept_name: How centripetal force changes when the radius changes but speed does not.

title: The Turning Bus and Inertia
question: When a bus rounds a sharp circular curve at constant speed, a standing passenger feels pushed outwards towards the exterior of the curve. Which of the following statements is physically correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="65" y="45" width="140" height="65" rx="12" fill="#b8cfe8" stroke="#2878c8" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="80" y="54" width="35" height="20" fill="#fff" stroke="#2878c8" /><rect x="120" y="54" width="35" height="20" fill="#fff" stroke="#2878c8" /><circle cx="92" cy="113" r="10" fill="#555" /><circle cx="178" cy="113" r="10" fill="#555" /><line x1="205" y1="78" x2="260" y2="78" stroke="#16856b" stroke-width="3" /><polygon points="267,78 255,72 255,84" fill="#16856b" /><text x="214" y="65" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Motion</text><line x1="135" y1="78" x2="135" y2="22" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="135,15 129,27 141,27" fill="#d97706" /><text x="145" y="27" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Inward acceleration</text></svg>

options.text: A real outward force accelerates the passenger away from the centre.
The passenger's inertia resists the change in direction of motion, while the bus undergoes inward acceleration.
Gravity acts horizontally towards the outside of the curve.
The bus has zero acceleration because its speed is constant.

explanation: Even at constant speed, the bus changes direction continuously and undergoes centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre of the curve. The standing passenger, due to inertia of direction, tends to continue in a straight line, which feels like an outward push relative to the accelerating frame of the bus.
concept_name: Inertia and acceleration during turning motion.

title: The Rotating Satellite
question: A communication satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at constant speed. Which of the following statements correctly describes the force acting on it and the nature of its motion?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="150" cy="80" r="52" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4" /><circle cx="150" cy="80" r="17" fill="#d6b77b" stroke="#806b44" stroke-width="2" /><text x="136" y="84" font-size="10" fill="#333">Earth</text><rect x="195" y="70" width="20" height="18" fill="#2878c8" stroke="#174a7c" /><line x1="205" y1="79" x2="150" y2="80" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><polygon points="143,80 155,74 155,86" fill="#d97706" /><text x="216" y="76" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Satellite</text><text x="167" y="68" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Gravity</text></svg>

options.text: Earth's gravitational force increases its speed continuously.
The satellite has no acceleration because its speed is constant.
Earth's gravitational force provides centripetal acceleration, changing the direction of velocity.
The satellite's velocity is directed towards Earth at every instant.

explanation: Earth's gravitational attraction acts towards its centre and provides the necessary centripetal force for circular orbital motion. In a circular orbit, the satellite's speed is constant, but the direction of its velocity vector changes continuously, resulting in centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre of the Earth.
concept_name: Gravity as the centripetal force for orbital motion.
